newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK Government acts as PLA troops cause fourth stir.
newsitem.headline: HK Government acts as PLA troops cause fourth stir.

text.p: The Hong Kong government moved swiftly to allay public concern on Wednesday that Chinese soldiers had taken up security duties a week before Britain hands the territory to Beijing.
Excited photographers snapped a contingent of mainland troops at the newly-built June 30 handover venue, believing they were highly-trained security experts inspecting the area.
But they were simply members of a People's Liberation Army (PLA) orchestra set to join the planned festivities, the government said, insisting that only police controlled security.
The incident caused a stir -- the fourth involving the PLA in Hong Kong in as many weeks, prompting newspapers to suggest the military get media-trained aides to avoid misunderstandings.

Hong Kong's government-in-waiting was handed a twin victory on Wednesday after the United States extended trading privileges to China and a British attempt to organise a boycott of its swearing-in ceremony crumbled.

News that the U.S. House of Representatives had voted to renew Beijing's Most Favoured Nation (MFN) trading status for another year was a major boost to Hong Kong, which lives off trade with the mainland.

The new government of Hong Kong, which Britain hands to China in a midnight ceremony, will be freed from fears of being caught in the middle of a trade war between the world's most populous and most powerful nations.
Separately, Washington announced that its consul general in Hong Kong would attend the investiture of the Beijing-picked legislature that will push aside a democratically-elected body.
U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright reaffirmed she would still shun the event, but Britain's bid to organise an international boycott lay in tatters.
A British Foreign Office spokesman in Hong Kong indicated that London, too, may relent and send an official -- although not visiting Prime Minister Tony Blair or Foreign Secretary Robin Cook.

The unannounced public appearance of Chinese troops in Hong Kong brought a quick comment from authorities. "It is the sole responsibility of the Hong Kong police to ensure the safety of the venue of the handover ceremony," a police spokesman said.

About 30 members of the PLA orchestra, wearing distinctive new casual clothing issued to the elite members of the future Hong Kong garrison, were conducted around the hall at the Convention and Exhibition Centre as workmen rushed to put the finishing touches to the building.
The troops declined to comment to waiting reporters but a police source said they had expressed satisfaction with what they saw.

China has sent 196 soldiers to Hong Kong as an advance party of the PLA's future garrison, and a further 500 will arrive a few hours before the handover, with thousands more set to move in shortly afterwards.

Those here already include an honour guard and orchestra to perform at the grand midnight ceremony when Britain's Prince Charles will hand Hong Kong back to China's President Jiang Zemin, ending 156 years of colonial rule.
Many in Hong Kong have a negative view of the PLA because of its role in crushing China's 1989 democracy movement.

The PLA has figured in three other incidents that triggered public unease. A general tried to pass through a closed border area and accused customs officials of an insult when turned back, but the government later blamed this on a language mixup.
The general spoke Mandarin and officials spoke Cantonese.
Then the PLA upset local residents near a barracks when it moved to shut down two civilian bus routes nearby. Another misunderstanding - officials said later.
In a bizarre incident two days ago a photographer was manhandled while witnessing 30 PLA troops marching out of a Bank of China branch with silver boxes that looked like weapons crates.
The confusion was smoothed over after a diplomat suggested the boxes contained only special presentation weapons to be used by the ceremonial honour guard.
